# The Museum of Unfinished Things

On my first morning at the Museum of Unfinished Things, the director handed me a key, a pencil, and half a biscuit.

“The key is for the front door,” she said. “The pencil is for the register. The biscuit is because I thought I wanted a whole one.”

Her name was Mrs. Vale. She wore a yellow cardigan whose left cuff had been repaired with green wool. In a museum devoted to incompletion, this seemed an unexpectedly firm statement.

The building had once been a railway station. Trains no longer stopped in our town, but the waiting room remained, along with its brown benches and a clock that showed twenty past four. Whether it was morning or afternoon had been debated by volunteers for years.

“We don’t mend the clock,” Mrs. Vale explained.

“Because it’s an exhibit?”

“Because the electrician quoted nine hundred pounds.”

I had applied for the job after leaving the planning office, where I had spent eleven years approving extensions to houses I would never enter. The museum offered less money, uncertain heating, and the possibility that work might occasionally surprise me.

“What exactly do we collect?” I asked.

Mrs. Vale led me past the ticket window into a room crowded with cabinets.

“Things people couldn’t finish. Things they wouldn’t finish. Things they simply stopped wanting.”

“And how do you tell the difference?”

“Usually we can’t.”

She gave me the larger portion of the biscuit.

“That,” she said, “is why we keep a register.”

I opened it carefully.

***

Our first exhibit was a model ship without a mast. Its donor, a retired dentist, had worked on it every Sunday for fourteen years before discovering that he preferred Sundays without it.

Beside it stood a wedding cake made of painted plaster. The baker had intended it for her shop window, then abandoned the business to become a driving instructor. According to her donation form, this had worked out extremely well.

There were unfinished novels, incomplete chess games, a quilt consisting of seventeen beautiful squares, and a brass instrument that three visiting musicians had failed to identify.

One cabinet contained a single glove.

“Surely that’s lost property,” I said.

“Look closer.”

It had six fingers.

In the former parcel office, shelves held things that people had asked us not to display: letters, sketchbooks, a dissertation, a list of baby names. These were wrapped in plain paper and identified only by numbers.

“Why keep them if nobody sees them?”

“People like knowing there’s somewhere they can be.”

I thought she meant the objects. Later I wondered.

My duties were modest. I dusted, catalogued donations, answered questions, and persuaded visitors not to complete the crossword displayed beneath glass.

One man came every Thursday to inspect a half-carved wooden fox. He never spoke or paid admission, which was voluntary anyway.

“Did he make it?” I asked.

“No.”

“Does he know who did?”

“I don’t think so.”

“What does he want?”

Mrs. Vale watched him through the doorway.

“A fox, perhaps. Must everything be complicated?”

***

After six weeks, I brought something of my own.

It was a blue cardigan my mother had begun knitting when I was nineteen. The back was finished, along with one sleeve and most of the front. The remaining wool lived in a plastic bag from a supermarket that no longer existed.

I had carried that bag through four flats, a marriage, a divorce, and the purchase of a small house whose dining room I used for drying laundry.

My mother was alive and well in a coastal town, where she attended swimming classes and complained about the price of cherries. Yet the cardigan had acquired, in my mind, the solemnity of something recovered from a shipwreck.

“She stopped when her hands got bad,” I told Mrs. Vale.

“Have you asked whether she wants it back?”

“She’ll only feel guilty.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

I telephoned my mother that evening.

“The blue thing?” she said. “Good heavens. Have you still got that?”

“I thought you might want me to keep it.”

“Whatever for?”

“Because you made it.”

“I also made a fish pie on Tuesday. You needn’t preserve that.”

I sat down on the stairs.

“Was it your hands?”

“What?”

“Why you stopped.”

“Oh, darling, no. The pattern was horrible. Those enormous shoulders. You’d have looked like a municipal building.”

For years I had imagined her setting down the needles in pain, reluctantly conceding something to age.

Outside her kitchen window, somebody called her name.

“Must go,” she said. “We’re going dancing.”

***

The closure notice arrived in November, folded into thirds.

The council owned the station. The roof leaked, the heating system was failing, and fewer than eight hundred people had visited the museum that year. Of these, Mrs. Vale admitted, several hundred might have been schoolchildren counted enthusiastically.

We had until the end of March to present a viable plan or vacate the premises.

I read the letter twice.

“They can’t just close it.”

“They can,” Mrs. Vale said. “It belongs to them.”

“But these things matter.”

“Yes. So does the roof.”

I wanted an adversary with polished shoes and no imagination. Instead, the council sent a woman called Denise, who arrived on a bicycle and kept her coat on throughout the meeting.

She inspected the damp patch above the quilt.

“My son made a castle out of cereal boxes,” she said. “It lived in our hall for three years. Eventually it had to go.”

“This isn’t a cereal-box castle,” I said.

“No,” she replied. “It’s a building with asbestos in the boiler room.”

After she left, I complained that she hadn’t understood us.

Mrs. Vale was putting a saucepan beneath a fresh leak.

“I think she understood us perfectly.”

That was worse.

I spent the afternoon drafting a statement about cultural memory. It contained the words *irreplaceable*, *community*, and *legacy* several times.

Mrs. Vale read it without expression.

“Will it bring in money?”

“Probably not.”

“Will it stop rain?”

“No.”

“Then perhaps begin again.”

I disliked her intensely until about half past five.

***

My first idea was a sponsored finishing marathon.

Local craftspeople would complete selected objects while visitors watched. We would auction the results, attract newspaper coverage, and prove that the collection possessed practical value.

Mrs. Vale asked who would choose what should be finished.

“We would.”

“Why?”

“Because we’re the museum.”

She waited.

I heard myself.

The second idea was worse: visitors could pay to have their abandoned ambitions ceremonially absolved. I had even written a slogan before realizing we would essentially be selling expensive permission slips.

For three days I sulked behind the ticket window.

Then the man who visited the fox approached my desk.

“Are you closing?”

“Possibly.”

“What happens to everything?”

“We don’t know.”

He looked toward the carving.

“My brother had one like that.”

“A fox?”

“A knife.”

He showed me with his hands: the length of the blade, the shape of the handle.

“We used to carve things behind the garage. Mostly terrible things.”

“Does your brother still carve?”

“He lives in Perth. I should ask.”

That evening I called a meeting of the volunteers. Seven people came, bringing nine packets of biscuits. I abandoned my prepared speech.

“What would you miss?” I asked.

“The people,” said Arthur, who polished the display cases.

“The quiet,” said Leila, who ran school visits.

“The excuse to leave the house,” said someone else.

Mrs. Vale said nothing.

Finally, I asked her.

She glanced around the room.

“I’d miss having somewhere to put things while I decide.”

I wrote that down too.

***

We held our first sorting day in January.

Not a finishing marathon. Not an auction. We invited donors, relatives, craftspeople, librarians, and anyone who had ever wondered what became of something they gave away.

The invitation said: **Help us decide what happens next.**

I expected twenty people. Sixty-three arrived.

The retired dentist reclaimed his ship. He had acquired a grandson who enjoyed wrecks.

The driving instructor took the plaster cake for her new office.

“It’ll make people ask questions,” she said.

A woman identified the mysterious brass instrument as part of a milking machine.

There was disappointment, followed by considerable relief.

The letters proved more difficult.

Some donors wanted theirs returned unopened. Others authorized us to destroy them. One man stood beside the shredder while I fed in eleven pages addressed to his former business partner.

“Do you want to say anything?” I asked.

“No,” he said. “That was the problem originally.”

We shredded them.

By lunchtime, I understood that I had been treating every object as a promise whose maker had failed to keep it.

But here were people recovering materials, correcting records, changing their minds.

The woman who had donated the quilt squares inspected them with a frown.

“These are good,” she said.

“They’re beautiful.”

“I know. I’d forgotten.”

She took twelve home and gave five to the school.

At four, the fox visitor returned with a photograph of his brother, aged twelve, holding something that might have been a wooden submarine.

“He says hello,” the man told me.

***

Not everyone approved.

A columnist accused us of dismantling the town’s heritage under the guise of public participation. A woman called to say museums were supposed to preserve things, not invite people to take them home.

She had a point.

We had already declined to destroy the notebooks of a local botanist, despite his nephew’s request. The incomplete observations contained the earliest recorded appearance of a marsh orchid in the county.

The nephew said his uncle would have preferred a clean desk.

The county ecologist said otherwise.

For a week, the notebooks sat between two chairs in my office while I tried to find a policy that could settle the matter. There wasn’t one. We arranged a meeting.

Mrs. Vale seemed almost cheerful.

“Now you’re doing museum work.”

“I thought I was doing that before.”

“Before, you were dusting.”

At the meeting, the nephew admitted that he had never read the notebooks. The ecologist admitted that she wanted them mainly for six pages. We agreed to digitize those pages, offer the originals to the county archive, and return the family photographs tucked into the covers.

Nobody got everything they wanted.

Afterward, Denise visited again. I showed her the lists: objects returned, transferred, retained, destroyed. She spent a long time reading the notes.

“How much space would you need,” she asked, “if you stopped trying to keep everything?”

I looked around my office. For the first time, it seemed possible to answer with a number.

I found a ruler in the desk.

***

The library had a room behind its local history shelves.

It was smaller than our parcel office, with fluorescent lights and a view of the supermarket loading bay. There was no ancient clock, no ticket window, no beautiful echo when rain struck the station roof.

It was dry.

Denise offered us the room for a year, provided we found volunteers and accepted a strict limit on storage.

Mrs. Vale measured it herself.

“We’ll fit,” she said.

“The collection won’t.”

“No.”

I waited for her to explain how this was secretly good.

She didn’t.

We spent February making choices. Some were easy. Others felt like betrayals, particularly when nobody wanted an object whose label I knew by heart.

A half-built dollhouse went to the recycling centre after three charities declined it. Its wallpaper had been cut from real wallpaper samples. Inside a tiny kitchen cupboard, I found a pencilled shopping list.

Milk. Bread. Apples.

I kept the cupboard longer than I should have, then asked a volunteer to drive me to the tip.

That night I took my mother’s cardigan out of its bag.

The wool was softer than I remembered.

I could finish it badly, pay someone to finish it well, or continue storing it until another person inherited the decision.

Instead, I rang my mother.

“Would you mind if I unravelled it?”

“Not at all. Save the buttons.”

“There aren’t any buttons.”

“Well, that shows how much I remember.”

We talked while I worked. Her evening class had started ballroom.

***

Unravelling required more patience than I expected.

The wool caught at seams and broke where moths had found it. Some sections came apart with a steady pull; others resisted until I laid them flat beneath a lamp and examined each knot.

My mother told me about her dance partner, a widower who counted aloud and apologized to furniture after bumping into it.

I told her about the museum.

“Are you disappointed?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Will you keep the job?”

“Some of it. Fewer hours.”

“Can you manage?”

“I think so.”

She did not tell me that everything happened for a reason. This was one of her better qualities.

By midnight, I had six uneven balls of wool and a small heap of unusable scraps.

I donated four balls to the library’s knitting group. I kept two, without a plan for them.

On the station’s last open day, we served tea in paper cups. People walked through the remaining exhibits, noticing spaces where familiar objects had stood.

The fox was still there.

Its Thursday visitor had declined to take it.

“I liked coming to see it,” he explained. “Having it on my mantelpiece wouldn’t be the same.”

We had agreed to bring it to the library.

Near closing time, Mrs. Vale stood beneath the broken clock.

“Will you miss this place?” I asked.

“Very much.”

She reached into her bag and produced a screwdriver.

“What are you doing?”

“Taking out the battery.”

“You said it was broken.”

“It is. Still no reason.”

***

We opened the new room on a Tuesday.

The library gave us a cabinet, two tables, and a noticeboard. Our name occupied a modest sign beside the door: **The Unfinished Room**.

Mrs. Vale insisted we were no longer large enough to call ourselves a museum.

Arthur insisted that size had nothing to do with it.

Their argument continued through lunch, which made the place feel settled.

We kept the fox, the six-fingered glove, the botanist’s digitized pages, and a changing selection of objects borrowed rather than acquired. There was a shelf for materials people could take, and a monthly afternoon when volunteers helped mend things.

Not everything was eligible. We learned to say no.

A boy brought in a cardboard bridge he had abandoned because his guinea pig refused to cross it.

“Do you want to finish it?” I asked.

“No. He can just walk around.”

“What would you like us to do?”

He considered this.

“Have you got any scissors?”

We cut the bridge into pieces suitable for making a tunnel.

Across the room, the fox visitor was telling Arthur about his brother’s garden in Perth. Mrs. Vale sorted buttons into an old biscuit tin. Outside, a delivery driver reversed toward the supermarket, his warning signal audible through the closed window.

At five, I entered the day’s donations in our new register.

Under the bridge, I wrote: *Returned to owner, altered.*

Then I put away the pencil, checked that the windows were shut, and went home before it got dark.
